chapters.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter XII
paragraphs: When they all drove back from Pelageya Danilovna's, Natasha — who always noticed everything — arranged it so that she and Madame Schoss rode in the sleigh with Dimmler, while Sonya rode with Nicholas and the maids.

On the way back Nicholas drove at a steady pace instead of racing, and kept peering in that fantastical, all-transforming light into Sonya's face, searching beneath the eyebrows and mustache for the old Sonya and the new one — the Sonya from whom he had resolved never to be parted again. He looked, and recognizing in her both the old and the new Sonya, and reminded by the smell of burnt cork of the sensation of her kiss, he inhaled the frosty air with a full chest and, gazing at the ground flying beneath him and the sparkling sky, felt himself in fairyland again.
"Sonya, is it well with you?" he asked from time to time.
"Yes!" she replied. "And with you?"
Halfway home Nicholas handed the reins to the coachman and ran over to Natasha's sleigh for a moment, standing on its running board.
"Natasha!" he whispered in French. "Do you know — I've made up my mind about Sonya."
"Have you told her?" asked Natasha, suddenly beaming all over with joy.
"Oh, how funny you look with that mustache and those eyebrows!... Natasha — are you glad?"

"I'm so glad, so glad! I was starting to be annoyed with you. I didn't say it, but you've been treating her badly. She has such a heart, Nicholas! I'm horrible sometimes, but I was ashamed to be happy while Sonya wasn't," continued Natasha. "Now I'm so glad! Well, run back to her."

"No, wait a moment... Oh, how funny you look!" cried Nicholas, peering into her face and finding in his sister too something new, unusual, and bewitchingly tender that he had not seen in her before. "Natasha, it's magical, isn't it?"
"Yes," she replied. "You've done the right thing."
"Had I seen her before the way she is now," thought Nicholas, "I would have asked her long ago what to do, and done whatever she told me, and everything would have been fine."
"So you're glad, and I've done right?"

"Oh, absolutely! I had a quarrel with Mama about it a while back. Mama said Sonya was trying to catch you. How could she say that! I nearly exploded at Mama. I will never let anyone say anything bad about Sonya, because there is nothing in her but good."

"Then it's all right?" said Nicholas, scrutinizing his sister's expression one more time to make sure she was serious. Then he jumped down, his boots crunching in the snow, and ran back to his sleigh. The same happy, smiling Circassian — with the mustache and beaming eyes peering up from under a sable hood — was still sitting there, and that Circassian was Sonya, and that Sonya was certainly his future happy and loving wife.

When they got home and told their mother how they had spent the evening at the Melyukovs', the girls went to their bedroom. After undressing — but without washing off the cork mustaches — they sat up for a long time talking about their happiness. They discussed how they would live after they were married, how their husbands would be friends, and how happy they would be. On Natasha's table stood two mirrors that Dunyasha had set up earlier.
"Only — when will all that happen? I'm afraid it never will... It would be too good!" said Natasha, getting up and going to the mirrors.
"Sit down, Natasha — maybe you'll see him," said Sonya.
Natasha lit candles, one on each side of one of the mirrors, and sat down.
"I see someone with a mustache," said Natasha, seeing her own face.
"You mustn't laugh, miss," said Dunyasha.

With Sonya's help and the maid's, Natasha got the mirror she was holding into the right position facing the other; her face took on a serious expression and she sat still. She sat a long time, gazing at the receding line of candle reflections in the mirrors, expecting — based on stories she had heard — to see either a coffin or him, Prince Andrew, in that last dim, indistinctly outlined square. But ready as she was to mistake the tiniest speck for the image of a man or a coffin, she saw nothing. She began blinking rapidly and moved away from the mirrors.
"Why do other people see things and I don't?" she said. "You sit down now, Sonya. You absolutely must tonight! Do it for me... Tonight I feel so frightened!"
Sonya sat down before the mirrors, found the right position, and began looking.
"Miss Sonya is sure to see something," whispered Dunyasha; "while you just laugh."
Sonya heard this and Natasha's whisper:
"I know she will. She saw something last year."
For about three minutes all were silent.
"Of course she will!" whispered Natasha — but didn't finish... because suddenly Sonya pushed away the mirror she was holding and covered her eyes with her hand.
"Oh, Natasha!" she cried.
"Did you see? Did you? What was it?" exclaimed Natasha, holding up the mirror.

Sonya had not actually seen anything; she had been about to blink and get up when she heard Natasha say "Of course she will!" She didn't want to disappoint either Dunyasha or Natasha, but it was hard to keep sitting still. She didn't know herself how or why the exclamation escaped her when she covered her eyes.
"You saw him?" Natasha pressed, seizing her hand.
"Yes. Wait a moment... I... saw him," Sonya managed to say, not yet sure whether Natasha meant Nicholas or Prince Andrew by "him."
"But why shouldn't I say I saw something? Others see things! And besides, who can tell whether I saw anything or not?" flashed through Sonya's mind.
"Yes, I saw him," she said.
"How? Standing or lying down?"
"No, I saw... At first there was nothing, then I saw him lying down."
"Andrew lying down? Is he sick?" asked Natasha, fixing her frightened eyes on her friend.
"No, on the contrary — on the contrary! His face was cheerful, and he turned toward me." And as she said this, she began to believe she really had seen what she described.
"Well, and then, Sonya?..."
"After that I couldn't make it out — there was something blue and red..."

"Sonya! When will he come back? When will I see him! Oh God, how afraid I am — for him and for myself and about everything!..." Natasha cried, and without waiting for Sonya's comforting words, she got into bed. Long after her candle was out she lay open-eyed and motionless, gazing at the moonlight streaming through the frosty windowpanes.

chapters.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter XIII
paragraphs: Soon after the Christmas holidays Nicholas told his mother of his love for Sonya and his firm resolve to marry her. The countess, who had long noticed what was going on and had been expecting this declaration, listened in silence and then told her son he could marry whom he pleased, but that neither she nor his father would give their blessing to such a marriage. Nicholas, for the first time, felt that his mother was displeased with him and that despite her love she would not yield. Coldly, without looking at her son, she sent for her husband, and when he came she tried — briefly and coolly, in their son's presence — to inform him of the facts. But she couldn't restrain herself and burst into tears of frustration, and left the room. The old count began half-heartedly to lecture Nicholas and beg him to give up the idea. Nicholas replied that he could not go back on his word, and his father, sighing and clearly uncomfortable, soon fell silent and went in to the countess. In all his dealings with his son, the count was always conscious of his own guilt toward him for having wasted the family fortune, and so he couldn't bring himself to be angry at Nicholas for refusing to marry an heiress and choosing the dowerless Sonya. On this occasion he was simply more acutely aware than ever that if their finances hadn't been in such disarray, no better wife for Nicholas than Sonya could have been wished for, and that no one but himself — with his Mitenka and his careless ways — was to blame for their situation.

The father and mother did not bring up the matter again with their son, but a few days later the countess sent for Sonya and, with a cruelty neither of them expected, reproached her niece for trying to catch Nicholas and for ingratitude. Sonya listened silently with downcast eyes, not understanding what was being demanded of her. She was ready to sacrifice everything for her benefactors. Self-sacrifice was her most cherished ideal — but in this case she couldn't see what she should sacrifice, or for whom. She couldn't help loving the countess and the whole Rostov family, but neither could she help loving Nicholas and knowing that his happiness depended on that love. She was silent and sad and made no reply. Nicholas sensed the situation was unbearable and went to have it out with his mother. He first begged her to forgive him and Sonya and consent to their marriage, then he threatened that if Sonya was mistreated he would marry her in secret.

The countess, with a coldness her son had never seen in her before, replied that he was of age, that Prince Andrew was marrying without his father's blessing and he could do the same — but that she would never accept that schemer as her daughter.

Stung by the word schemer, Nicholas raised his voice and told his mother he had never expected her to try to force him to sell his feelings — but that if that was how it was, he would say once and for all... But he didn't have time to say the decisive word whose expression on his face his mother was awaiting with terror, and which might have remained a cruel memory between them forever. He didn't have time to say it because Natasha, with a pale, set face, came in through the door where she had been listening.
"Nicholas, you're talking nonsense! Be quiet — be quiet — be quiet, I tell you!..." she almost screamed, drowning out his voice.

"Mama darling, it's not like that at all... my poor, sweet darling," she said to her mother, who — realizing they had been on the brink of a rupture — looked at her son with terror, but in the stubbornness and heat of the conflict could not and would not back down.
"Nicholas, I'll explain things to you. Go away! Listen, Mama darling," said Natasha.
Her words were incoherent, but they achieved their purpose.
The countess, sobbing heavily, buried her face on her daughter's chest, while Nicholas got up, clutched his head, and left the room.

Natasha set about making peace, and succeeded well enough that Nicholas extracted a promise from his mother that Sonya would not be troubled, while he for his part promised not to do anything without his parents' knowledge.

Firmly resolved — after putting his regimental affairs in order — to resign from the army and return home to marry Sonya, Nicholas left at the beginning of January to rejoin his regiment. He was serious, sorrowful, and at odds with his parents, but convinced, as it seemed to him, that he was passionately in love.
After Nicholas left, things in the Rostov household grew more depressing than ever, and the countess fell ill from the emotional strain.

Sonya was unhappy at being separated from Nicholas and still more so at the hostile tone the countess could not help adopting toward her. The count was more worried than ever by the state of their finances, which demanded some drastic action. The town house and the estate near Moscow would inevitably have to be sold, and for this they needed to go to Moscow. But the countess's illness forced them to keep postponing their departure from day to day.

Natasha, who had borne the first period of separation from her fiance lightly and even cheerfully, now grew more restless and impatient with each passing day. The thought that her best days — which she would have spent loving him — were being wasted to no purpose tormented her constantly. His letters mostly irritated her. It hurt her to think that while she lived only in thoughts of him, he was living a real life, seeing new places and new people that interested him. The more interesting his letters were, the more annoyed she felt. Her letters to him, far from giving her any comfort, felt like a tedious and artificial obligation. She couldn't write, because she couldn't imagine expressing in a letter even a thousandth part of what she could convey with her voice, her smile, and her eyes. She wrote him formal, monotonous, dry letters to which she herself attached no importance, and the countess corrected her spelling mistakes in the rough drafts.

There was still no improvement in the countess's health, but postponing the trip to Moscow any longer was impossible. Natasha's trousseau had to be ordered and the house sold. Moreover, Prince Andrew was expected in Moscow, where old Prince Bolkonsky was spending the winter, and Natasha was sure he had already arrived.
So the countess stayed in the country, and the count, taking Sonya and Natasha, went to Moscow at the end of January.

chapters.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter I
paragraphs: After Prince Andrew's engagement to Natasha, Pierre suddenly felt — without any apparent reason — that it was impossible to go on living as before. Firmly convinced as he was of the truths revealed to him by his benefactor, and happy as he had been in perfecting his inner self, to which he had devoted himself with such passion — all the meaning of such a life vanished after Andrew's engagement and the death of Joseph Alexeevich, the news of which reached him almost simultaneously. Only the skeleton of life remained: his house, a brilliant wife who now enjoyed the favors of a very important personage, acquaintance with all of Petersburg, and his court service with its dull formalities. And this life suddenly seemed unbearably loathsome to Pierre. He stopped keeping a diary, avoided the Brothers, began going to the club again, drank heavily, and fell back in with the bachelor crowd, leading such a life that Countess Helene thought it necessary to scold him severely about it. Pierre felt she was right, and to avoid embarrassing her he left for Moscow.

In Moscow, as soon as he entered his huge house where the faded and aging princesses still lived with their enormous household; as soon as he drove through the city and saw the Iberian shrine with its countless candles burning before the golden icon covers, the Kremlin Square with its undisturbed snow, the cabbies and hovels of the Sivtsev Vrazhok — those old Muscovites who wanted nothing, hurried nowhere, and were peacefully living out their days; when he saw the old Moscow ladies, the Moscow balls, and the English Club — he felt himself at home in a quiet haven. In Moscow he felt at peace, at home, warm and slovenly as in an old dressing gown.

Moscow society, from the grandmothers down to the children, received Pierre like a long-awaited guest whose place was always ready and waiting. For Moscow society Pierre was the nicest, kindest, smartest, jolliest, and most generous of eccentrics — a heedless, good-natured nobleman of the old Russian type. His purse was always empty because it was open to everyone.

Benefit concerts, bad paintings, statues, charitable societies, gypsy choirs, schools, subscription dinners, drinking bouts, Freemasons, churches, and books — nothing and no one ever met with a refusal from him, and if it hadn't been for two friends who had borrowed large sums and taken him under their wing, he would have given everything away. There was never a dinner or soiree at the club without him. As soon as he sank into his spot on the sofa after two bottles of Margaux, people gathered around and the talking, arguing, and joking began. When quarrels broke out, his kindly smile and well-timed jokes reconciled the opponents. The Masonic dinners were dreary and dull when he wasn't there.

When, after a bachelor supper, he got up with his amiable, kindly smile and yielded to entreaties to go off somewhere with the revelers, shouts of delight and triumph arose among the young men. At balls he danced whenever a partner was needed. Young ladies, married and unmarried, liked him because he was equally friendly to all without making love to any of them, especially after supper. "He's charming; he has no sex," they said of him.
* "He is charming; he has no sex."
Pierre was one of those hundreds of retired gentlemen-in-waiting who were good-naturedly living out their days in Moscow.

How horrified he would have been seven years earlier, when he first came back from abroad, if someone had told him there was no need for him to seek or plan anything, that his groove had long been carved, predetermined from eternity, and that no matter how he wriggled he would become what everyone in his position became. He could not have believed it! Hadn't he once longed with all his heart to establish a republic in Russia; then to be a Napoleon; then a philosopher; then a strategist and the conqueror of Napoleon? Hadn't he seen the possibility of, and passionately desired, the regeneration of sinful humanity and his own rise to the highest perfection? Hadn't he established schools and hospitals and freed his serfs?

But instead of all that — here he was, the wealthy husband of an unfaithful wife, a retired gentleman-in-waiting, fond of eating and drinking and of — as he unbuttoned his waistcoat — grumbling about the government; a member of the Moscow English Club and a universal favorite in Moscow society. For a long time he couldn't reconcile himself to the idea that he had become one of those very same retired Moscow gentlemen-in-waiting he had so despised seven years ago.

Sometimes he consoled himself with the thought that he was only living this way temporarily; but then he was startled by the realization that how many others, like him, had entered this life and this club "temporarily" — with a full head of teeth and hair — and had only left when not a single tooth or hair remained.

In moments of pride, when he reflected on his position, it seemed to him that he was quite different from and distinct from those other retired gentlemen-in-waiting he had formerly looked down on: they were empty, stupid, self-satisfied fellows, content with their lot, "while I am still dissatisfied and want to do something for humanity. But perhaps all these comrades of mine struggled just as I did, looking for something new, a path of their own — and like me were brought by force of circumstances, of society, of upbringing, by that elemental force against which man is powerless, to the same state I'm in," he told himself in moments of humility. And after living in Moscow for a while he no longer despised but began to grow fond of, respect, and pity his fellows in fate, just as he pitied himself.

Pierre no longer suffered those acute bouts of despair, self-loathing, and disgust with life. But the same illness that had once expressed itself in those violent attacks was now driven inward and never left him for a moment. "What for? Why? What is going on in the world?" he would ask himself several times a day, perplexed, involuntarily starting to ponder the meaning of things anew. But knowing from experience that there were no answers to these questions, he quickly turned away from them and picked up a book, or hurried off to the club or to Apollon Nikolaevich's to swap the latest gossip.

"Helene, who has never cared about anything except her own body and is one of the stupidest women alive," thought Pierre, "is regarded by people as the pinnacle of intelligence and refinement, and they worship her. Napoleon Bonaparte was despised by everyone as long as he was great, but now that he has become a pathetic comedian, Emperor Francis wants to offer him his daughter in an illegal marriage. The Spaniards, through the Catholic clergy, offer thanks to God for their victory over the French on the fourteenth of June — and the French, also through the Catholic clergy, give thanks for defeating the Spaniards on that same fourteenth of June. My brother Masons swear by their blood that they are ready to sacrifice everything for their neighbor, but they won't give a ruble each to charity, and they scheme — the Astraea Lodge against the Manna Seekers — and fuss over an authentic Scottish carpet and a charter that nobody needs and whose very author doesn't understand. We all profess the Christian law of forgiving injuries and loving our neighbors — the law in whose honor we've built forty times forty churches in Moscow — but yesterday a deserter was flogged to death, and a minister of that same law of love and forgiveness gave the soldier a cross to kiss before his execution." So thought Pierre, and this whole universal deception — which everyone accepted, accustomed as they were to it — astonished him afresh each time, as if it were something new. "I see the deception and confusion," he thought, "but how am I to tell them all that I see? I have tried, and I've always found that they too, deep in their souls, understand it as I do — they just try not to look. So it seems this is how things must be! But I — what is to become of me?" he thought. He had the unfortunate capacity — common among men, especially Russians — of seeing and believing in the possibility of goodness and truth, but of seeing the evil and falsehood of life too clearly to be able to take any serious part in it. Every sphere of activity was connected, in his eyes, with evil and deception. Whatever he tried to be, whatever he took up, the evil and falsehood repelled him and blocked every path. Yet he had to live and find something to do. It was too terrible to exist under the burden of these unsolvable problems, so he abandoned himself to every distraction in order to forget them. He went everywhere, drank a great deal, bought paintings, took up construction, and above all — read.

He read, and read everything that came to hand. On coming home, while his valets were still helping him undress, he would pick up a book and start reading. From reading he passed to sleeping, from sleeping to gossip at drawing rooms and the club, from gossip to drinking and women, from drinking back to gossip, reading, and wine. Drinking became more and more both a physical and a moral necessity. Though the doctors warned him that wine was dangerous for someone of his weight, he drank heavily. He only felt fully at ease when, having mechanically poured several glasses of wine into his large mouth, he felt a pleasant warmth in his body, an amiability toward everyone, and a readiness to respond to any idea without probing it too deeply. Only after a bottle or two did he feel dimly that the terribly tangled skein of life that had previously horrified him was not as dreadful as he had thought. He was always vaguely aware of some thread of that skein, buzzing in his head after dinner or supper, while chatting, listening, or reading. But under the influence of wine he would tell himself: "It doesn't matter. I'll untangle it. I have a solution worked out, but I don't have time right now — I'll think it all through later." But the "later" never came.
In the morning, on an empty stomach, all the old questions looked as insoluble and terrible as ever, and Pierre hastily picked up a book. And if someone came to visit, he was glad.

Sometimes he recalled how he had heard that soldiers in war, when trapped under enemy fire with nothing to do, try hard to find some occupation to make it easier to bear the danger. To Pierre, all people seemed like those soldiers, seeking refuge from life: some in ambition, some in cards, some in lawmaking, some in women, some in toys, some in horses, some in politics, some in sport, some in wine, some in government affairs. "Nothing is trivial and nothing is important — it's all the same — only to escape from it as best one can," thought Pierre. "Only not to see it — that dreadful it!"

chapters.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter II
paragraphs: At the beginning of winter, Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky and his daughter moved to Moscow. At that time, enthusiasm for Emperor Alexander's regime had waned and a patriotic, anti-French sentiment prevailed. This, combined with the old prince's record, his intellect, and his eccentricity, immediately made Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky an object of particular respect among Muscovites and the center of Moscow's opposition to the government.

The prince had aged greatly that year. He showed unmistakable signs of senility: a tendency to fall asleep at odd moments, forgetfulness of recent events, sharp recall of distant ones, and the childish vanity with which he embraced the role of head of the Moscow opposition. Despite this, the old man inspired the same feeling of respectful awe in every visitor — especially in the evenings when he appeared for tea in his old-fashioned coat and powdered wig and, prompted by someone, would tell his brusque stories of the past or deliver even more brusque and scathing judgments of the present. For them all, that old-fashioned house with its huge mirrors, pre-Revolution furniture, powdered footmen, and the stern, shrewd old man — himself a relic of the past century — with his gentle daughter and the pretty Frenchwoman, both reverently devoted to him, presented a majestic and charming spectacle. But the visitors didn't consider that besides the couple of hours during which they saw their host, there were twenty-two other hours in the day when the private, intimate life of the household went on.

That private life had lately become very hard for Princess Mary. Here in Moscow she was deprived of her greatest comforts — her conversations with the pilgrims and the solitude that restored her at Bald Hills — and she had none of the advantages and pleasures of city life. She didn't go out in society; everyone knew her father wouldn't let her go anywhere without him, and his failing health prevented him from going out, so she wasn't invited to dinners or parties. She had completely given up hope of getting married. She saw the coldness and contempt with which the old prince received and dismissed the young men who sometimes appeared at their house as possible suitors. She had no friends: during this visit to Moscow she had been disappointed in the two people who had been closest to her. Mademoiselle Bourienne, with whom she had never been entirely open, had now become unpleasant to her, and for various reasons Princess Mary avoided her. Julie, with whom she had corresponded for five years, turned out to be completely alien when they met in person. Julie — who had become one of Moscow's wealthiest heiresses through the death of her brothers — was deep in the whirl of society pleasures. She was surrounded by young men who, she fancied, had suddenly learned to appreciate her worth. Julie was at that stage in a society woman's life when she feels that her last chance of marrying has come and her fate must be decided now or never. On Thursdays Princess Mary recalled with a sad smile that she now had no one to write to, since Julie — whose presence gave her no joy — was right here in Moscow, and they saw each other weekly. Like the old emigre who declined to marry the lady with whom he'd spent his evenings for years, she regretted Julie's presence and missed having someone to write to. In Moscow, Princess Mary had no one to talk to, no one to confide in — and much sorrow had recently fallen on her. The time for Prince Andrew's return and marriage was approaching, but his request that she prepare their father for it had not been carried out; in fact, things seemed quite hopeless — at every mention of the young Countess Rostova the old prince, who was usually in a bad temper anyway, lost all self-control. Another recent sorrow arose from the lessons she gave her six-year-old nephew. To her dismay she detected in herself, when dealing with little Nicholas, symptoms of her father's irritability. No matter how often she told herself she must not lose patience while teaching her nephew, almost every time she sat down with pointer in hand to show him the French alphabet, she so desperately wanted to pour her own knowledge quickly into the child — who was already afraid that Auntie might get angry at any moment — that at the slightest inattention she would tremble, become flustered and heated, raise her voice, and sometimes grab him by the arm and stand him in the corner. Having put him there she would cry over her own cruel, wicked nature, and little Nicholas, following her example, would sob, and without permission would leave his corner, come to her, pull her wet hands from her face, and comfort her. But what distressed the princess most of all was her father's irritability, which was always directed at her and had lately come close to cruelty. Had he forced her to prostrate herself on the ground all night, had he beaten her or made her haul firewood and water, it would never have entered her mind to think her lot was hard; but this loving tyrant — all the more cruel because he loved her and tormented himself on her account — knew how not merely to hurt and humiliate her deliberately, but to make her feel that she was always to blame for everything. Lately he had developed a new trait that tormented Princess Mary more than anything: his growing closeness to Mademoiselle Bourienne. The notion that had occurred to him as a joke when he first learned of his son's plans — that if Andrew married, he himself would marry Bourienne — had evidently pleased him, and lately he had been persistently, as it seemed to Princess Mary solely to wound her, showing the companion exaggerated affection and expressing displeasure with his daughter through demonstrations of love for Bourienne.

One day in Moscow, in Princess Mary's presence — she believed her father did it on purpose when she was there — the old prince kissed Mademoiselle Bourienne's hand and, pulling her close, embraced her tenderly. Princess Mary flushed and ran from the room. A few minutes later Mademoiselle Bourienne came into Princess Mary's room, smiling and chatting in her pleasant voice. Princess Mary quickly wiped away her tears, went resolutely up to Mademoiselle Bourienne, and — evidently unaware of what she was doing — began shouting in angry haste at the Frenchwoman, her voice breaking: "It's horrible, vile, inhuman — to take advantage of weakness..." She didn't finish. "Get out of my room," she cried, and burst into sobs.

The next day the prince didn't say a word to his daughter, but she noticed that at dinner he ordered Mademoiselle Bourienne to be served first. After dinner, when the footman brought the coffee and from habit started with the princess, the prince flew into a sudden rage, threw his stick at Philip the footman, and immediately gave orders for him to be sent into the army.

"He doesn't obey... I said it twice... and he doesn't obey! She is the first person in this house; she is my best friend," the prince shouted. "And if you allow yourself," he screamed, addressing Princess Mary for the first time, "to forget yourself again in her presence as you did yesterday, I will show you who is master in this house. Now go! And don't let me see you again — beg her pardon!"
Princess Mary asked Mademoiselle Bourienne's forgiveness, and also her father's forgiveness for herself and for Philip the footman, who had begged her to intercede.

At such moments something like a pride of sacrifice gathered in her soul. And then suddenly that same father she had judged would begin groping for his spectacles in her presence, fumbling near them but not finding them, or would forget something that had just happened, or would take a false step with his failing legs and turn to see if anyone had noticed his weakness, or — worst of all — would suddenly fall asleep at dinner when there were no guests to stimulate him, letting his napkin slip and his trembling head droop over his plate. "He is old and feeble, and I dare to judge him!" she would think at such moments, with a wave of self-reproach.

chapters.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter III
paragraphs: In 1811 there lived in Moscow a French doctor named Metivier who had rapidly become fashionable. He was enormously tall, handsome, charming in the French manner, and was, as all Moscow said, an extraordinarily clever physician. He was received in the best houses not merely as a doctor but as an equal.

Prince Nicholas had always ridiculed medicine, but lately, on Mademoiselle Bourienne's advice, he had allowed this doctor to visit him and had grown accustomed to him. Metivier came to see the prince about twice a week.

On December 6th — St. Nicholas's Day and the prince's name day — all Moscow came to the prince's door, but he gave orders to admit no one and to invite to dinner only a small number of guests whose names he gave Princess Mary.

Metivier, who came that morning with his congratulations, considered it proper in his capacity as doctor to force his way past the barrier, as he explained to Princess Mary, and went in to see the prince. It happened that on this name-day morning the prince was in one of his worst moods. He had been going around the house since dawn finding fault with everyone and pretending not to understand what was said to him and not to be understood himself. Princess Mary knew this mood of quiet, absorbed grouchiness well — it generally built to an explosion of rage — and she went about all morning as though walking past a loaded gun, waiting for the inevitable shot. Until the doctor's arrival the morning had passed safely. After admitting the doctor, Princess Mary sat in the drawing room with a book near the door through which she could hear everything from the study.
* To force the barrier.

At first she heard only Metivier's voice, then her father's, then both speaking at once. The door was flung open and on the threshold appeared the handsome figure of the terrified Metivier with his shock of black hair — and behind him the prince in his dressing gown and fez, his face contorted with fury and the pupils of his eyes rolled down.
"You don't understand?" the prince shouted. "But I do! French spy, Bonaparte's lackey — spy — get out of my house! Out, I tell you!" And he slammed the door.
Metivier shrugged his shoulders and went up to Mademoiselle Bourienne, who had rushed in from the next room at the sound of shouting.
"The prince is not feeling well: a bilious attack and a rush of blood to the head. Don't worry, I'll call again tomorrow," said Metivier; and putting his fingers to his lips, he hurried away.
Through the study door came the sound of shuffling slippers and the cry: "Spies, traitors, traitors everywhere! Not a moment's peace in my own house!"

After Metivier left, the old prince called his daughter in, and the full weight of his fury fell on her. She was to blame for letting a spy in. Hadn't he told her — yes, told her — to make a list, and not admit anyone who wasn't on it? Then why was that scoundrel allowed in? She was the cause of it all. With her, he said, he couldn't have a moment's peace and couldn't die in peace.

"No, madam! We must part — we must part! I want you to understand that — I cannot endure this any longer," he said, and left the room. Then, as if afraid she might find some means of consolation, he came back and — trying to appear calm — added: "And don't think I said this in a fit of temper. I am calm. I've thought it over, and this will be carried out: we must part. Find yourself somewhere to live..." But he couldn't hold himself back, and with the fury that only someone who loves is capable of — clearly suffering himself — he shook his fists at her and screamed:
"If only some fool would marry her!" Then he slammed the door, sent for Mademoiselle Bourienne, and shut himself up in his study.
At two o'clock the six chosen guests assembled for dinner.

These guests — the famous Count Rostopchin, Prince Lopukhin with his nephew, General Chatrov (an old war comrade of the prince's), and from the younger generation Pierre and Boris Drubetskoy — waited for the prince in the drawing room.

Boris, who had come to Moscow on leave a few days earlier, had been eager to be presented to Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky and had managed to ingratiate himself so well that the old prince made an exception to his rule of not receiving bachelors.

The prince's house did not belong to fashionable society, but his small circle — though not much talked about in town — was more flattering to be received in than any other. Boris had realized this the week before, when the commander-in-chief invited Rostopchin to dinner on St. Nicholas's Day in his presence, and Rostopchin had replied that he couldn't come:
"On that day I always go to pay my respects to the relics of Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky."
"Oh, yes, yes!" the commander-in-chief had replied. "How is he?..."

The small group that gathered before dinner in the lofty, old-fashioned drawing room with its antique furniture resembled the solemn assembly of a court of law. Everyone was silent or spoke in low tones. Prince Nicholas entered looking serious and taciturn. Princess Mary seemed even quieter and more reserved than usual. The guests were reluctant to address her, sensing she was in no mood for conversation. Count Rostopchin alone kept the talk alive, sharing the latest town news and political gossip.

Lopukhin and the old general occasionally joined in. Prince Bolkonsky listened like a presiding judge receiving reports, now and then silently or with a brief word indicating that he was taking note. The tone of the conversation made clear that no one approved of what was happening in the political world. Stories were told that obviously confirmed the view that everything was going from bad to worse — but each speaker stopped, or was stopped, at the point where criticism might touch the sovereign himself.
At dinner the conversation turned to the latest political news: Napoleon's seizure of the Duke of Oldenburg's territories and the hostile Russian Note sent to all European courts.

"Bonaparte treats Europe like a pirate treats a captured ship," said Count Rostopchin, repeating a phrase he had used many times. "One can only marvel at the patience — or the blindness — of the crowned heads. Now it's the Pope's turn, and Bonaparte doesn't scruple to depose the head of the Catholic Church — yet everyone keeps silent! Our sovereign alone has protested against the seizure of the Duke of Oldenburg's territory, and even..." Rostopchin paused, feeling he had reached the boundary beyond which criticism was not permitted.

"Other territories have been offered in exchange for the Duchy of Oldenburg," said Prince Bolkonsky. "He shuffles dukes around the way I might move my serfs from Bald Hills to Bogucharovo or my Ryazan estates."
"The Duke of Oldenburg bears his misfortune with admirable strength and dignity," Boris remarked, joining in respectfully.

He said this because on his trip from Petersburg he had had the honor of being presented to the Duke. Prince Bolkonsky glanced at the young man as if about to say something, but changed his mind — evidently considering him too young.
"I've read our protest about the Oldenburg affair and was surprised at how poorly the Note was worded," said Count Rostopchin, in the casual tone of a man speaking on a familiar subject.
Pierre looked at Rostopchin with naive surprise, not understanding why the wording of the Note should bother him.
"Does it matter, Count, how the Note is worded," he asked, "as long as its substance is forceful?"
"My dear fellow, with five hundred thousand troops it should be easy to have good style," replied Count Rostopchin.
Pierre now understood the count's dissatisfaction with the wording of the Note.

"One would have thought there were enough pen-pushers around," remarked the old prince. "Over there in Petersburg they're always scribbling — not just notes but new laws too. My Andrew has written a whole volume of laws for Russia. Everything is writing nowadays!" And he laughed his unnatural laugh.
There was a momentary pause; the old general cleared his throat to draw attention.
"Did you hear about the latest incident at the review in Petersburg? The impression made by the new French ambassador."
"Oh? Yes, I heard something: he said something awkward in His Majesty's presence."

"His Majesty directed attention to the Grenadier division and the march past," the general continued, "and it seems the ambassador paid no attention and took the liberty of replying: 'We in France pay no attention to such trifles!' The Emperor did not condescend to reply. At the next review, they say, the Emperor did not once deign to address him."
All were silent. On this point, which concerned the Emperor personally, no judgment could be passed.

"Impudent scoundrels!" said the prince. "You know Metivier? I threw him out of my house this morning. He was here — they let him in despite my orders that no one was to be admitted," he said, glancing angrily at his daughter.
And he told the whole story of his conversation with the French doctor and the reasons that convinced him Metivier was a spy. Though the reasons were flimsy and unclear, no one raised an objection.
After the roast, champagne was served. The guests rose to congratulate the old prince. Princess Mary also went up to him.

He gave her a cold, angry look and offered her his wrinkled, clean-shaven cheek to kiss. His whole expression told her he had not forgotten the morning's conversation, that his decision stood, and only the presence of guests kept him from saying so now.
When they moved to the drawing room for coffee, the older men sat together.
Prince Nicholas grew more animated and shared his views on the coming war.

He said that our wars with Bonaparte would be disastrous as long as we sought alliances with the Germans and meddled in European affairs, into which we had been dragged by the Treaty of Tilsit. "We ought not to fight either for or against Austria. Our political interests all lie in the East, and as for Bonaparte — all that's needed is an armed frontier and a firm policy, and he will never dare cross the Russian border, as he proved in 1807!"

"How can we fight the French, Prince?" said Count Rostopchin. "Can we take up arms against our teachers and our gods? Look at our young people, look at our ladies! The French are our gods: Paris is our Kingdom of Heaven."
He began speaking louder, clearly intending to be heard by everyone.

"French fashions, French ideas, French feelings! There — you threw Metivier out by the scruff of his neck because he's a Frenchman and a scoundrel, but our ladies crawl after him on their knees. I went to a party last night, and out of five women three were Catholics with papal dispensation to do needlework on Sundays. And they themselves sit around practically naked, like the signboards at our public bathhouses, if you'll pardon the comparison. Ah, when one looks at our young people, Prince, one would like to dig out Peter the Great's old cudgel from the museum and thrash them in the good old Russian way until all the nonsense is beaten out of them."
Everyone was silent. The old prince looked at Rostopchin with a smile and nodded approvingly.
"Well, goodbye, your excellency — keep well!" said Rostopchin, getting up with his characteristic briskness and holding out his hand to the prince.
"Goodbye, my dear fellow... His words are music — I never tire of hearing them!" said the old prince, keeping hold of his hand and offering his cheek to be kissed.
Following Rostopchin's example, the other guests also rose.
